passages.title: Island Ferry: timetable and fares
paras: Island Ferry operates a passenger and vehicle service between Port Ellis and Carrow Island all year round. From April to September there are six crossings a day in each direction; from October to March this is reduced to four. The crossing takes approximately 45 minutes, although it may take longer in rough weather.

Foot passengers do not need to book and may simply buy a ticket at the terminal up to ten minutes before departure. Vehicles, however, must be booked in advance, either online or by phone, as space on the car deck is limited. Vehicles should arrive at least 30 minutes before departure; those arriving later may lose their place.

A single adult ticket costs £8, and a return £14. Children aged 5 to 15 travel at half price, and children under five travel free. Bicycles are carried free of charge. The fare for a car with up to two passengers is £45 return. Frequent travellers can save money with a book of ten single tickets, which costs £60 and is valid for six months.

Dogs are welcome but must be kept on a lead at all times and are not allowed in the indoor lounge. Refreshments are available on board on all crossings, but the café on the upper deck opens only during the summer timetable.

Sailings may be cancelled at short notice in severe weather. Passengers are advised to check the website or our social media pages before travelling. If your sailing is cancelled, your ticket will be valid on the next available crossing, or you may request a full refund.

passages.title: Part-time Customer Service Assistant – Brightwell Home Stores
paras: Brightwell Home Stores is looking for a friendly and reliable Customer Service Assistant to join the team at our Kingsgate branch. The role is part-time, 20 hours per week, with shifts including at least one weekend day.

Your main responsibilities will be to welcome customers, answer questions about our products, and process returns and exchanges at the customer service desk. You will also deal with telephone enquiries and help to arrange home deliveries for large items such as furniture.

Previous experience in retail is an advantage but is not essential, as full training will be provided. What matters most is a positive attitude, good communication skills and the ability to stay calm when dealing with difficult situations. Basic computer skills are required.

We offer a competitive hourly rate, a 20% discount on all purchases for staff and their immediate family, and the opportunity to progress to a supervisor role. Staff who work for us for more than a year are also offered free first-aid training.

To apply, please complete the online form on our careers page and attach a short covering letter explaining why you would like to work with us. CVs sent by post will not be accepted. The closing date is 28 May, and interviews will be held in the first week of June.

passages.title: Staff handbook: requesting annual leave
paras: All full-time employees are entitled to 25 days of paid annual leave per year, in addition to public holidays. Part-time employees receive leave in proportion to the hours they work. The leave year runs from 1 January to 31 December.

Requests for leave should be made through the staff portal. Please give at least four weeks’ notice for periods of more than five working days, and at least one week’s notice for shorter periods. Your line manager will normally respond within three working days.

Because we need to maintain enough staff at all times, managers may refuse a request if too many people in the same team have already booked leave for the same dates. Requests are dealt with in the order in which they are received, so it is a good idea to book popular periods, such as school holidays, as early as possible.

Up to five days of unused leave may be carried over into the following year, but these must be taken by the end of March. Any other unused leave will be lost. In exceptional circumstances, such as long-term illness, your manager may agree to a longer carry-over period.

If you need time off at very short notice because of a family emergency, contact your manager by phone as soon as possible rather than using the portal. Such absences may be recorded as emergency leave rather than deducted from your annual entitlement.

passages.title: A brief history of the umbrella
paras: Today the umbrella is one of the most ordinary objects we own, so common that millions are lost or thrown away every year. Yet for most of its long history it was a luxury item and a symbol of status, and its use for keeping off the rain is a relatively recent development.

The earliest umbrellas, which appeared several thousand years ago in the ancient civilisations of the Middle East, Asia and North Africa, were designed to provide shade from the sun. Carved images show servants holding parasols over the heads of kings and nobles. In many societies, the right to be shaded in this way was restricted to people of high rank, and the size and decoration of a parasol indicated how important its owner was.

It was in China that the umbrella first became waterproof. Craftsmen there are thought to have coated paper or silk canopies with wax and lacquer, producing a device that offered protection from rain as well as sun. Chinese umbrellas also introduced a collapsible frame of bamboo ribs, so that the umbrella could be closed when it was not needed. This basic design has changed surprisingly little since then.

In Europe, umbrellas were rare for many centuries. When they did appear, they were largely regarded as accessories for women. For a man to carry one in the rain was considered a sign of weakness, or even of poverty, since it suggested that he could not afford to travel by carriage. Wealthy men preferred to wear heavy coats and hats and to accept getting wet.

Attitudes began to change in Britain in the eighteenth century. One traveller who had seen umbrellas used abroad is said to have carried one through the streets of London for many years, ignoring the laughter and insults of passers-by. Carriage drivers were especially hostile, since they feared that umbrellas would reduce the demand for their services. Gradually, however, the practical advantages won people over, and by the end of the century umbrellas had become common among men as well as women.

The nineteenth century brought important technical improvements. Early European umbrellas were heavy, with ribs made of wood or whalebone, and could weigh several kilograms. The introduction of a frame made from thin steel ribs made umbrellas lighter, stronger and cheaper to produce. As factories began to manufacture them in large numbers, the umbrella changed from a luxury into an everyday item that almost anyone could buy.

The twentieth century added the folding umbrella, small enough to fit in a handbag, and new waterproof fabrics such as nylon. Recent innovations include umbrellas designed to resist strong winds by allowing air to pass through vents in the canopy. Despite such improvements, the umbrella remains, in essence, the same simple device that Chinese craftsmen created centuries ago, a reminder that some designs are difficult to improve upon.
